To infantilize someone means to treat them as if they are a child — even though they are not. It means you act toward them as if they are less intelligent, less capable, or less mature than they actually are. In doing so, you take away — or ignore — their ability to think, decide, and act for themselves.

The word comes from infant, meaning a very young child. When you infantilize someone, you mentally "turn them into an infant" in the way you treat them.
What It Looks Like in Practice

Infantilizing doesn't always look the same. It can be subtle or very obvious. Here are the most common forms:

Making decisions for them without asking.
You decide what's best for someone instead of letting them decide for themselves. You assume they can't figure it out, so you just handle it for them — without their input.

Over-explaining things they already know.
You break things down far more than necessary, as if they've never encountered a simple idea before. You explain things slowly, repeatedly, or in an overly basic way that would be appropriate for a child but feels insulting to an adult.

Using baby talk or an exaggerated, soft tone.
You speak to them in a voice or with words that you'd use for a toddler — overly cheerful, soft, slow, or simplified. This is common, for example, when some people speak to the elderly or to those with disabilities.

Withholding information "for their own good."
You decide they can't handle the truth, the full story, or the complexity of a situation, so you hide it, soften it beyond recognition, or give them a watered-down version. You become their gatekeeper rather than trusting them to process information themselves.

Overprotecting them.
You constantly step in to prevent them from facing any difficulty, risk, or discomfort — because you don't believe they're capable of handling it. This stops them from growing, learning, or taking any ownership of their own life.

Dismissing their opinions or feelings.
You treat their thoughts as not worth seriously engaging with — the way an adult might wave off a child's argument as "cute" rather than responding to it with real respect.

In a family:
A parent continues to manage every aspect of their 30-year-old child's life — booking their appointments, handling their finances, telling them what to eat. The parent may love their child deeply, but they are infantilizing them by never trusting them to be a capable adult.

In healthcare:
A doctor explains a diagnosis to a patient's family member instead of talking directly to the patient. Or a doctor uses a soothing, over-simplified tone with an elderly patient who is mentally sharp — just because of their age. The patient is being infantilized.

In the workplace:
A manager never gives an employee any real responsibility, checks every small decision they make, and explains instructions as if the employee has never done anything before — even though they're experienced. That employee is being infantilized.

In media and advertising:
When a company's advertisement assumes its audience can't understand anything complex and dumbs content down to an almost insulting degree, it is infantilizing its audience. Or when a government constantly tells citizens what they should think or feel rather than presenting them with honest information and trusting them to form their own conclusions.

In a relationship:
A partner constantly speaks on behalf of the other person in social situations, answers questions directed at them, and makes all the household decisions — treating the other person like a dependent rather than an equal. That is infantilization.
Why It Matters — The Harm It Causes

Infantilizing someone is harmful for several reasons:

It strips dignity. Every adult has a right to be treated as a capable person. When someone infantilizes you, they are signaling — whether they mean to or not — that they see you as less than fully competent. This is deeply disrespectful.

It removes autonomy. Autonomy means the ability to make your own choices. When someone infantilizes you, they take that away. Over time, this can make a person feel powerless, dependent, and unsure of themselves.

It can create the very helplessness it assumes. If someone is constantly treated as incapable, they may begin to become more dependent over time. The infantilization creates the condition it was supposedly responding to — a vicious cycle.

It breaks trust. Being infantilized sends a message: "I don't trust you." That feeling of not being trusted by someone close to you — a parent, a doctor, a boss — is painful and damaging to the relationship.

This is an important distinction.

Sometimes infantilization is deliberate — used as a tool of control or power. By treating someone like a child, you keep them dependent on you. You position yourself as the authority, the wise one, the one in charge.

But more often, infantilization is well-meaning. People infantilize others out of love, protectiveness, or habit — without realizing how it comes across. A parent who still treats their adult child like a helpless 8-year-old may genuinely just love them and want to help. A nurse who uses baby talk with elderly patients may think she's being warm and kind.

The good intentions do not cancel the harm. The impact on the other person — the feeling of not being trusted, not being respected, not being seen as a capable adult — is real, regardless of what the person doing it intended.

The word can also point inward. A person can infantilize themselves — meaning they voluntarily act more helpless, dependent, or immature than they actually are. This might look like:

  • Refusing to take responsibility for decisions
  • Always relying on others to solve problems they could handle themselves
  • Avoiding any situation that requires them to act like a capable adult

This is sometimes a response to having been infantilized for a long time — people can internalize the message that they aren't capable.

If you want one sentence to anchor this word in your memory: to be infantilized is to be treated as less than the capable adult you are. The person on the receiving end typically feels a mix of frustration, humiliation, and powerlessness — not because they are being attacked, but because they are being underestimated in a way that feels just as bad.

Understanding these nearby words will sharpen your understanding:

To patronize — to treat someone as if they are less intelligent or important than you, often while pretending to be helpful or kind. Infantilizing often is patronizing, but patronizing is a broader term.

To condescend — to speak or behave as though you are superior to someone. Closely related, but condescension is more about tone and attitude, while infantilizing is specifically about treating someone as a child.

To coddle — to treat someone too gently, protecting them from any hardship. Coddling is one of the most common forms of infantilizing.

To undermine — to weaken someone's confidence or authority. Infantilizing often results in undermining someone.
